design_detail: Cross-sectional comparison of 471 online reports on the content of ecstasy tablets sold on the Dutch market, posted on Pillreports.net (218) and Partyflock.nl (253) between 1 January 2014 and 31 December 2015, with the database of the Dutch Drugs Information and Monitoring System (DIMS), which holds the GC–MS results, physical features, date and place of tablets handed in at Dutch drug-checking offices. Each report was compared with database entries for matching tablets submitted within 12 weeks before or after the report's date (p. 95). DIMS employees scored each report: MDMA amount 'too high' or 'too low' if it differed by more than 10 mg from the matching database entry (the average was used where a report gave a range); 'unreported substance' if similar database tablets in the window contained substances the report did not mention; 'dangerous' if the reported MDMA amount was more than 40 mg too low (for a range: its average 40 mg too low, or its maximum 40 mg below the database maximum) or if an unreported psychoactive substance was present in relevant amounts; and whether the report had a picture, gave a range of amounts ('spread inclusion'), and matched more than one distinct tablet in the database ('multiple database hits') (pp. 95–96). Frequencies with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (1000 samples), χ² tests and logistic regressions in SPSS 22 (p. 96). Filed as cross-sectional and appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for drug-checking data; the DIMS database is the reference standard and is not itself checked in this paper.
can_establish: How often online reports posted in 2014–2015 about ecstasy tablets on the Dutch market differed from what the Dutch drug-checking database recorded for matching tablets (amount of MDMA, other substances), and which visible features of a report went with fewer reports judged dangerous.
cannot_establish: How much the content of tablets with the same logo or look varies (the paper gives no figures and cites older data for it, p. 98); how accurate online reports are outside the Netherlands or after 2015; why reports were wrong (the explanations offered are untested, pp. 97–98); or what happened to people who relied on them.

sample.recruitment: Online reports about ecstasy tablets on the Dutch market, posted on Pillreports.net and Partyflock.nl between 1 January 2014 and 31 December 2015 and collected by hand (automated collection proved unreliable); the two sites were chosen because earlier DIMS monitoring of drug-related websites found them the most active on ecstasy tablet information (p. 95, Materials and methods › Design).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Reports concerning the Dutch market only; no reports older than 2014, because the market changes (p. 95). How many reports were found in all, how many were excluded, and what was done when no matching tablet was in the database within the 12-week window are not stated. Reports could not be classified by their own source (experience, home test, laboratory test): most named none, and the variable was dropped (p. 99).
sample.demographics: Not applicable: the units are online reports; who posted them is unknown.
sample.selection_effects: Two Dutch websites chosen as the most active; only reports about the Dutch market; the denominator of reports looked at is not given, so reports that could not be matched to the database may be missing. The authors note that people in the Netherlands are arguably better informed about drug content than elsewhere because of DIMS, and warn against extrapolating to other countries (p. 99).

exposure.measurement: Content of each report (MDMA amount or range, other substances, picture, description) compared by DIMS employees with DIMS database records of matching tablets (GC–MS composition, physical characteristics, date and place of submission) within 12 weeks before or after the report (p. 95, Procedure: comparison to the DIMS database).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (reports about tablets). Amounts are the MDMA content per tablet stated in a report and recorded in the database.
exposure.polysubstance: Substances other than MDMA appear only as 'unreported substances' found in matching database tablets; which substances they were is not listed.

comparison.controls: The DIMS database records for matching tablets serve as the reference; other comparisons are between the two websites and between reports with and without a picture or a range of amounts.
comparison.matching: A report was matched to database tablets on its description (and picture, where included) within ±12 weeks. Where several distinct tablets matched (10.8% of reports), how the comparison value was chosen is not stated.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not reported: how often reports had no database match; the spread of MDMA content within a matching batch; how close in time the matching database entry was; agreement between scorers.

outcomes.instruments: Predefined scoring rules applied by DIMS employees: concentration too high, concentration too low (each more than 10 mg from the database), concentration difference dangerous (more than 40 mg too low), unreported substance, unreported substance dangerous, dangerous (either kind), spread inclusion, picture inclusion, multiple database hits (pp. 95–96).
outcomes.validity_norms: No reliability data: the number of scorers, their blinding and their agreement are not reported. The DIMS database is called validated, without data (p. 95).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Dangerous' = reported MDMA more than 40 mg too low (for ranges: average 40 mg too low, or maximum 40 mg below the database maximum), or an unreported psychoactive substance present in relevant concentrations (p. 96). Overstatements by more than 40 mg were not counted as dangerous; the authors judged that risk too speculative to score (p. 98). 'Relevant concentrations' is not defined in numbers.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None across 18 tests of association: three χ² tests in the Results text, one further χ² (multiple hits against dangerous), Table 4 (three χ²) and the logistic regressions of Tables 2, 3 and 5 (11 terms).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; the scorers were DIMS employees comparing each report with the DIMS database, so they saw both.

analysis.effect_sizes: Reported MDMA amounts were on average 10.6 mg higher than the database (95% CI 6.7–14.4; no SD or distribution given) (p. 96). Frequencies with 95% bootstrap CIs (Table 1, p. 97): too high 39.7% (35.2–44.4); too low 17.6% (14.0–21.2); unreported substance 15.5% (12.3–18.9); dangerous 15.3% (11.9–18.5). Logistic regressions (Tables 2, 3, 5, p. 97): picture inclusion with multiple database hits Exp(b) 0.298 (0.111–0.799); multiple hits with a dangerous concentration difference 4.880 (1.608–14.81) and with an unreported substance 2.556 (1.056–6.186); spread inclusion with dangerous reports 0.511 (0.307–0.850). Editors' reconstruction from the Table 1 percentages, the site totals and the Table 4 χ² of 6.890: dangerous in 34 of 159 reports without a range (21.4%) and 38 of 312 with one (12.2%), a risk ratio of about 1.75 and an odds ratio of about 1.96 (the reconstruction reproduces χ² = 6.890 exactly).
analysis.covariates: The models of Tables 2 and 5 enter website, picture and (Table 5) spread inclusion together. Picture inclusion and website are strongly related (86.7% of Pillreports and 12.6% of Partyflock reports had a picture, Table 1); editors' calculation of their correlation: phi about 0.74, just below the authors' multicollinearity threshold of 0.80 (Tables 2, 5 notes).
analysis.selective_reporting: The report-source variable was dropped after scoring proved impossible (p. 99), and the statement that reports quoting DIMS laboratory tests were often false comes without numbers (p. 99). The share of reports within 10 mg of the database, and of reports giving no amount, is not reported.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 471 reports, the 95% intervals of the main percentages are about ±3 to ±5 percentage points.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 471 online reports from 2014–2015 about tablets on the Dutch market, 39.7% stated an MDMA amount more than 10 mg above the matching DIMS record and 17.6% more than 10 mg below it (on average 10.6 mg too high); 15.5% missed a substance found in matching tablets; 10.2% understated MDMA by more than 40 mg; 15.3% met the authors' definition of dangerous; 10.8% of reports matched more than one distinct tablet in the database. Reports giving a range of amounts were less often dangerous (about 12% against 21%, editors' reconstruction); a picture helped match a report to the right tablet but did not make reports less often dangerous.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract describes the 15.3% as reports that omit the relevant concentration spread, fail to report additional illegal or dangerous substances, or underestimate MDMA by more than 40 mg (p. 94); in the methods, giving no range is not itself a criterion (p. 96), and the abstract's criterion for unreported substances (illegal or dangerous in the database) differs from the methods' (a psychoactive substance in relevant concentrations, p. 96) and the discussion's (p. 98). The discussion and conclusion say reports without a range are 'approximately twice as likely' to be dangerous (pp. 98–99), which is the odds ratio; the risk ratio is about 1.75 (editors' calculation). The discussion explains the null result for pictures by similar-looking pills coming from different batches or producers with different contents (p. 98), which the study did not measure. The conclusion that online information tends to overestimate MDMA content (p. 99) is supported for these two Dutch sites in 2014–2015, and the authors themselves caution against extrapolating abroad (p. 99).

timeline.event: Cole et al. (2002), cited for older data showing that MDMA content can vary heavily between tablets with the same appearance (ref. 15, p. 98); not read here.
Brunt and Niesink (2011), the DIMS methods and results paper cited for the database (ref. 12, p. 95).
This study, published online in 2016 (print issue 2017); the authors describe it as, to their knowledge, the first study of the reliability of online information on ecstasy content (p. 99).

replication.where_it_stands: A single study of two Dutch websites in 2014–2015 by the team that runs DIMS. No replication on other websites, in other countries or in later years is cited.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors are at the Trimbos Institute, which runs DIMS, the reference database (p. 94), and the discussion argues for DIMS-like systems (p. 99). A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A study that collects tablets matching online reports (logo, picture and description as given) in several countries and years, analyses each tablet in the laboratory, and reports how often the online amount and substances were right, together with the spread of content among tablets with the same logo.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Two Dutch websites chosen as the most active on ecstasy tablets: a frame for these sites in 2014–2015, not for online drug information in general.
All reports about the Dutch market in the period appear to have been taken, but how many were found and how many were excluded (for example for want of a database match) is not stated.
471 reports; the 95% intervals of the main percentages are about ±3 to ±5 percentage points.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Websites, period and scoring rules are described; the reports' own sources (experience, home test, laboratory) could not be classified.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Reports without a database match, and the choice of comparison value when several database tablets matched, are not described.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: GC–MS-based DIMS records are a strong reference, but matching rests on each report's description within ±12 weeks, and the 10-mg and 40-mg thresholds are the authors' choices.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The rules were predefined, but the number of scorers, their blinding and agreement are not reported, and 'relevant concentrations' is undefined.

Bootstrap intervals suit the frequencies; but the P values of Table 4 do not match its χ² values, the website row of Table 5 duplicates that of Table 2, an odds ratio is described as 'twice as likely', and there is no correction across 18 tests.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A clear comparison of online reports with a laboratory-based reference, but the number of reports looked at, the handling of unmatched or multiply matched reports and the reliability of the scoring are not reported, and several statistics are misprinted. Citable for: in 2014–2015, on the two most active Dutch sites, about 4 in 10 online reports about a tablet overstated its MDMA content by more than 10 mg and about 1 in 6 understated it by more than 10 mg; about 1 in 7 reports missed another substance in matching tablets; about 1 in 7 were wrong in a way the authors call dangerous; reports giving a range of amounts were less often dangerously wrong; a picture helped identify the tablet but did not make reports safer. Not citable for: how much tablets with the same logo vary in content, the accuracy of online reports in other countries or years, or why reports were wrong.

key_findings.finding: Design and sample: 471 online reports about ecstasy tablets on the Dutch market, 218 from Pillreports.net and 253 from Partyflock.nl, posted from 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2015, each compared by DIMS employees with DIMS database records (GC–MS) of matching tablets handed in within 12 weeks before or after the report.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Design, single paragraph; Procedure: comparison to the DIMS database, single paragraph (p. 95); Measures: scoring method, single paragraph (pp. 95–96)

key_findings.finding: Reported MDMA amounts were on average 10.6 mg higher than the database (95% CI 6.7–14.4); Pillreports gave too-high amounts more often than Partyflock (χ² = 10.86, P = 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Frequencies of scored variables, single paragraph

key_findings.finding: Frequencies (Table 1, all reports, 95% bootstrap CIs): MDMA amount more than 10 mg too high 39.7% (35.2–44.4); more than 10 mg too low 17.6% (14.0–21.2); more than 40 mg too low 10.2% (7.6–13.0); unreported substance 15.5% (12.3–18.9); unreported substance judged dangerous 7.0% (4.7–9.3); dangerous overall 15.3% (11.9–18.5). Too high: 47.7% of Pillreports and 32.8% of Partyflock reports; dangerous: 14.7% and 15.8%.
key_findings.note: Counts reconstructed from the percentages and the site totals are consistent throughout (for example too high 187 of 471, dangerous 72 of 471; editors' calculation). The share within 10 mg of the database, or giving no amount, is not reported; by subtraction it is at most 42.7% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: A report's description matched more than one distinct tablet in the database in 10.8% of reports (5.5% on Pillreports, 15.4% on Partyflock). The authors take this to mean that several different pills on the market fit the description, so a reader could not tell them apart from the report alone. Including a picture went with fewer such multiple matches (Exp(b) 0.298, 95% CI 0.111–0.799, P = 0.016).
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Measures: scoring method (p. 96, left column); Table 1 and Table 2 (p. 97)

key_findings.finding: Reports with multiple database matches more often understated MDMA by more than 40 mg (Exp(b) 4.880, 95% CI 1.608–14.81, P = 0.005) and more often missed a substance (2.556, 1.056–6.186, P = 0.037), but not significantly more often missed a dangerous substance (1.514, 0.477–7.225, P = 0.481); multiple matches went with reports being judged dangerous overall (χ² = 34.26, P < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of multiple database hits, single paragraph (pp. 96–97); Table 3 (p. 97)
key_findings.note: The interval 0.477–7.225 is not symmetric around 1.514 on the log scale; the printed P fits an upper limit of about 4.8 (editors' calculation; see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Giving a range of amounts (done in 66.2% of reports) was the only visible report feature associated with fewer dangerous reports (Exp(b) 0.511, 95% CI 0.307–0.850, P = 0.010; χ² = 6.890); including a picture (Exp(b) 1.044, 0.490–2.225) and the website (1.104, 0.517–2.356) were not.
key_findings.locator: Results › Dangerous report characteristics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1; Tables 4 and 5
key_findings.note: Editors' reconstruction from Table 1 and the χ² of 6.890: dangerous in 34 of 159 reports without a range (21.4%) against 38 of 312 with one (12.2%), a risk ratio of about 1.75 and an odds ratio of about 1.96. The authors' 'approximately twice as likely' (pp. 98–99) is the odds ratio.

key_findings.finding: For errors in the stated MDMA amount, only understatements (more than 40 mg too low) were scored as dangerous: the authors considered whether reports overstating MDMA by more than 40 mg should also count, judged that risk too speculative to score, and so left the commonest error (overstatement) out of 'dangerous'. (An unreported psychoactive substance could also make a report dangerous.)
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Criteria used for the scoring of dangerous reports, single paragraph (begins at the foot of the left column, continues in the right column)

key_findings.finding: The authors expected a picture to make reports safer and found it did not. They suggest, without testing it, that similar-looking pills can come from different batches or producers with different amounts and even different substances, and that the 12-week window probably filtered out most multiple matches, so a picture may matter more for a tablet without recent reports.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Characteristics of dangerous reports and multiple database hits, single paragraph

key_findings.finding: On how much tablets of the same look vary, the authors say recent figures are not available and cite older data (ref. 15, Cole et al., 2002) showing that content can vary heavily between tablets with the same appearance; from this they argue that the 40-mg threshold could be reached when a report gives no range.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Incorrect notation of concentrations and tablet substance, 1st paragraph (begun on p. 97; this part on p. 98, left column); reference 15 (p. 100)

key_findings.finding: Explanations offered for the overstatement, which the authors say the data cannot test: dealers posting false reports to advertise their product, and people estimating content from their own experience.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Incorrect notation of concentrations and tablet substance, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors tried to score each report's source (experience, home test, laboratory test) and gave up: most reports named no source, and where DIMS laboratory tests were quoted as the source, the stated amounts were often not found in the database (no numbers given).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Relevance and remarks, single paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: because of DIMS, people in the Netherlands are arguably better informed about drug content than elsewhere, so the findings should be extrapolated to other countries with care; the lack of DIMS-like systems elsewhere makes similar studies difficult.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Relevance and remarks, single paragraph; Conclusion, single paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The website row of Table 5 (Exp(b) 1.104, 95% CI 0.517–2.356, P = 0.799) is identical to the website row of Table 2, although the two models have different outcomes (dangerous reports in Table 5, multiple database hits in Table 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two rows is probably a copying error; the website's association with one of the two outcomes is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The P values of Table 4 (0.472, 0.007, 0.417) do not correspond to its Pearson χ² values with one degree of freedom (0.040, 6.890, 0.116). In the editors' calculation those χ² values give two-sided P of about 0.84, 0.009 and 0.73, while the printed P values match one-sided Fisher exact tests on 2×2 tables reconstructed from Table 1, which the table does not say.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the conclusions do not change, but the table pairs a statistic with P values from another test.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods state one-tailed significance for the logistic regressions (p. 96), but the P values in Tables 2, 3 and 5 match two-sided Wald tests computed from the printed confidence intervals (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the stated test direction is not the one reported.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3 the interval for 'unreported substance dangerous' (Exp(b) 1.514, 0.477–7.225) is not symmetric around its estimate on the log scale, unlike every other interval in Tables 2, 3 and 5; the printed P of 0.481 fits an upper limit of about 4.8 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The upper limit is probably misprinted; the association is non-significant either way.

reporting_issues.issue: Three different definitions of a 'dangerous' unreported substance: listed as illegal or dangerous in the DIMS database and present in relevant quantities (abstract, p. 94); a psychoactive substance present in relevant concentrations (methods, p. 96); present in a relevant concentration and/or a pill containing something completely different from the report (discussion, p. 98). 'Relevant' is never given in numbers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which unreported substances counted as dangerous cannot be reproduced; cite the 7.0% and the 15.3% with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes the 15.3% as reports that omit the relevant concentration spread, fail to report substances or underestimate MDMA by more than 40 mg (p. 94); in the methods, a range counts only when its average or maximum is 40 mg below the database, and giving no range is not itself a criterion (p. 96).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the 15.3% with the methods' definition.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion and conclusion say reports without a range are 'approximately twice as likely' to be dangerous (pp. 98–99). That is the odds ratio: in the editors' calculation 1/0.511 is about 1.96, while reconstructed proportions give about 21% against 12%, a risk ratio of about 1.75.
reporting_issues.consequence: Say about 21 in 100 against 12 in 100 rather than twice as likely.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of reports found, excluded, or without a matching database tablet in the 12-week window is not reported, nor how the comparison value was chosen when several database tablets matched; the share of reports within 10 mg, or giving no amount, is not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominators behind the percentages cannot be checked, and the share of accurate reports is unknown (at most 42.7% by subtraction, editors' calculation).

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Addiction 112, 94–100: all pages (pp. 94–100, plus a copy-disclaimer page appended to the file); text extracted and every number checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; Tables 1–5 checked on the rendered p. 97; no figures; no supplement mentioned.

disagreements.first_pass: Only underestimates were scored as dangerous: the authors considered whether reports overstating MDMA by more than 40 mg should also count, judged that risk too speculative to score, and so left the commonest error (overstatement) out of 'dangerous'.
disagreements.reviewer: For errors in the stated MDMA amount, only understatements (more than 40 mg too low) were scored as dangerous: the authors considered whether reports overstating MDMA by more than 40 mg should also count, judged that risk too speculative to score, and so left the commonest error (overstatement) out of 'dangerous'. (An unreported psychoactive substance could also make a report dangerous.)
disagreements.resolution: Second reader's correction adopted by the AI co-editor (AI reader 778 (round-2 check))

disagreements.reviewer: The card's affiliations note (p. 94) and where_it_stands say the Trimbos Institute, or the authors' team, runs DIMS; the paper does not state this. It says only that all four authors are at the Trimbos Institute and that the scoring was done by DIMS employees (p. 95).
disagreements.resolution: Recorded for the card's next revision; not yet in the card.

disagreements.reviewer: The Results use causal verbs for cross-sectional associations: including a picture 'leads to' better tablet recognition (p. 96), and spread inclusion 'causes a significant difference' in dangerous scoring (p. 97).
disagreements.resolution: Recorded for the card's next revision; not yet in the card.
